use: For someone else's mother, and for your own mum when talking to her or at home.

example.ja: お母さん、今日のご飯何？
example.english: Mum, what's for dinner today?

examplePolite.ja: お母さんはお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your mother?

notes: With outsiders in polite talk, call your own mother haha.

use: For someone else's father, and for your own dad when talking to him or at home.

example.romaji: otousan, ashita no shiai mi ni kuru?
example.ja: お父さん、明日の試合見に来る？
example.english: Dad, are you coming to my game tomorrow?

examplePolite.ja: お父さんも来ますか？
examplePolite.english: Is your father coming too?

notes: With outsiders in polite talk, call your own father chichi.

use: Your own mother when talking to people outside the family; someone else's mother is okaasan.

example.romaji: haha ga kyou kotchi ni kuru n da
example.ja: 母が今日こっちに来るんだ
example.english: My mum's coming here today.

examplePolite.romaji: haha wa toukyou ni sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: 母は東京に住んでいます
examplePolite.english: My mother lives in Tokyo.

notes: Calling your own mother okaasan to a teacher or boss sounds childish.

use: Your own father when talking to people outside the family; someone else's father is otousan.

example.romaji: chichi wa mada shigoto da yo
example.ja: 父はまだ仕事だよ
example.english: My dad's still at work.

examplePolite.romaji: chichi wa ginkou de hataraite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 父は銀行で働いています
examplePolite.english: My father works at a bank.

notes: Calling your own father otousan to a teacher or boss sounds childish.

use: Your own family or families in general; someone else's family is gokazoku.

example.ja: 週末は家族と過ごす
example.english: I'm spending the weekend with my family.

examplePolite.ja: 家族は四人です
examplePolite.english: There are four of us in my family.

use: One or both parents, often parents in general; someone else's parents are oyagosan.

example.ja: やばい、親にバレた
example.english: Oh no, my parents found out.

examplePolite.ja: 親に相談しました
examplePolite.english: I talked it over with my parents.

use: Both your parents; someone else's are goryoushin.

example.ja: 両親に電話しなきゃ
example.english: I need to call my parents.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoushin wa oosaka ni sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: 両親は大阪に住んでいます
examplePolite.english: My parents live in Osaka.

use: Someone else's parents; the polite form of ryoushin.

example.romaji: kanojo no goryoushin ni au n da
example.ja: 彼女のご両親に会うんだ
example.english: I'm meeting my girlfriend's parents.

examplePolite.ja: ご両親はお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How are your parents?

use: Your own older brother when talking to others; someone else's is oniisan.

example.romaji: ani wa ima amerika ni iru
example.ja: 兄は今アメリカにいる
example.english: My big brother's in America now.

examplePolite.ja: 兄が一人います
examplePolite.english: I have one older brother.

notes: To his face you say oniichan or his name, never ani.

use: Someone else's older brother, or what you call your own to his face.

example.ja: お兄さんは今何歳？
example.english: How old is your brother now?

examplePolite.romaji: oniisan wa ima nansai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お兄さんは今何歳ですか？
examplePolite.english: How old is your brother now?

notes: Shop staff and strangers also use it to call a young man.

use: Your own older sister when talking to others; someone else's is oneesan.

example.romaji: ane ga raigetsu kekkon suru n da
example.ja: 姉が来月結婚するんだ
example.english: My big sister's getting married next month.

examplePolite.ja: 姉は看護師です
examplePolite.english: My older sister is a nurse.

notes: To her face you say oneechan or her name, never ane.

use: Someone else's older sister, or what you call your own to her face.

example.ja: お姉さんって優しいね
example.english: Your sister's so kind.

examplePolite.romaji: oneesan wa doko ni sunde imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お姉さんはどこに住んでいますか？
examplePolite.english: Where does your sister live?

notes: Also a friendly way to call a young woman, such as shop staff.

use: Brothers and sisters in general; the kanji says brothers but it covers sisters too.

example.ja: 兄弟は何人いるの？
example.english: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

examplePolite.ja: 兄弟が二人います
examplePolite.english: I have two siblings.

notes: Someone else's siblings are gokyoudai; hitorikko means an only child.

use: Your own younger sister; someone else's is imoutosan.

example.ja: 妹が風邪ひいちゃった
example.english: My little sister caught a cold.

examplePolite.ja: 妹は高校生です
examplePolite.english: My younger sister is in high school.

use: Your own younger brother; someone else's is otoutosan.

example.ja: 弟とゲームしてた
example.english: I was playing games with my little brother.

examplePolite.ja: 弟は大学生です
examplePolite.english: My younger brother is a university student.

notes: Don't mix it up with otousan (father).

use: Someone else's younger sister.

example.ja: 妹さんは今いくつ？
example.english: How old's your little sister now?

examplePolite.ja: 妹さんはお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your sister?

use: Someone else's wife; also a way to address a married woman.

example.ja: 奥さんは元気にしてる？
example.english: How's your wife doing?

examplePolite.romaji: okusan mo issho ni dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 奥さんも一緒にどうですか？
examplePolite.english: Why not bring your wife along too?

notes: Some men also say uchi no okusan for their own wife in casual talk.

use: Neutral word for your own wife; someone else's is okusan.

example.romaji: tsuma ga ninshin shita n da
example.ja: 妻が妊娠したんだ
example.english: My wife's pregnant.

examplePolite.romaji: tsuma to futari de sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: 妻と二人で住んでいます
examplePolite.english: I live with my wife, just the two of us.

notes: In casual talk many men say yome instead.

use: Neutral word for your own husband; someone else's is goshujin.

example.ja: 夫が料理してくれる
example.english: My husband does the cooking.

examplePolite.ja: 夫は会社員です
examplePolite.english: My husband is an office worker.

notes: In casual talk many women say danna instead.

use: Polite word for someone else's husband.

example.romaji: goshujin, nan no shigoto shiteru no?
example.ja: ご主人、何の仕事してるの？
example.english: What does your husband do?

examplePolite.ja: ご主人はお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your husband?

notes: Also the master or owner of a shop or house.
